translationRepairs: In Bu Xu's later years, the Xiahou clan's rule grew feeble. They abandoned Ji's teachings and grew neglectful. Bu Xu forfeited his position and fled among the Rong and Di peoples.
In Bu Xu's later years, the rule of the Xiahou clan declined; it abandoned the office of agriculture and neglected farming. Bu Xu thereby lost his post and fled among the Rong and Di peoples.
去稷不務 means the Xia court abandoned the agricultural office (稷) and neglected it; the English "Ji's teachings" invents a teaching and misreads the cause of Bu Xu losing his office.
Tai Jiang bore the youngest son Ji Li. Ji Li wed Tai Ren. Both were exemplary women who gave birth to Chang, attended by auspicious signs.
Tai Jiang bore the youngest son Ji Li. Ji Li wed Tai Ren. Both were worthy women. Tai Ren gave birth to Chang, attended by sage-like auspicious signs.
皆賢婦人 describes Tai Jiang and Tai Ren as worthy women, and 生昌 refers to Tai Ren bearing Chang; the English implies both women gave birth to Chang.
Yin's ancestor Yi heard of this and grew fearful. He informed Emperor Zhou.
Zu Yi of Yin heard of this and grew fearful. He informed Emperor Zhou.
祖伊 is the personal name of a Yin minister (Zu Yi); 殷之祖伊 does not mean "Yin's ancestor Yi".
Two years elapsed. He learned that Zhou's madness and cruelty had grown ever more extreme. He had slain Prince Bi Gan and imprisoned jizi.
Two years elapsed. He learned that Zhou's benighted disorder and cruelty had grown ever more extreme: he had slain Prince Bi Gan and imprisoned Jizi.
箕子 is the proper name Jizi and must be capitalized; 昏亂 means benighted disorder rather than madness.
Mao Shuzheng presented the purified water. Duke Kang of Wei spread the purple mats. Duke Zhao of Shao assisted with the rites. The venerable Jiang Ziya led the sacrificial beast.
Mao Shuzheng presented the purified water. Kang Shu Feng of Wei spread the mats. Shi, Duke of Shao, assisted with the offerings. The venerable Jiang Ziya led the sacrificial beast.
衛康叔封 is Kang Shu (Feng) of Wei, not a "Duke Kang"; 召公奭 is Shi, Duke of Shao; 茲 here are the mats and 采 the offerings.

Yin Qi beat the drum and pronounced the invocation: "Yin's final descendant Ji Zhou extinguishes and rejects the former kings' luminous virtue, affronts and scorns the gods without offerings, savagely oppresses the people of Shang city. His notorious crimes are manifestly heard by the August Heavenly Emperor."

Yin Yi read the invocation from the written tablets: "The last descendant of Yin, Zhou, has destroyed and cast aside the bright virtue of the former kings, insulted the spirits and gods and failed to sacrifice to them, and cruelly oppressed the people of the Shang city. His deeds are manifest and have been heard by the August Heaven and the Lord on High."
尹佚 is Yin Yi (not Yin Qi); 筴祝 means reading the prayer from written tablets, not beating a drum; 季紂 means the last scion Zhou, not a name "Ji Zhou"; 天皇上帝 is August Heaven and the Lord on High.
Then he ordered Duke Zhao to free jizi from captivity.
Then he ordered the Duke of Shao to free Jizi from captivity.
箕子 is the proper name Jizi (capitalized); 召公 is the Duke of Shao.
The king continued: 'Establish Heaven's safeguarding, dwell in Heaven's sanctuary. Thoroughly identify the wicked, depose those who served and received from the Shang king.
The king continued: 'Secure Heaven's protection and rely on Heaven's house. Seek out all the wicked and demote those who followed Shou, the king of Yin.
殷王受 is King Zhou of Yin by his personal name Shou; the clause means demoting those who followed him, not "those who served and received from the Shang king".
King Wu had already overthrown the Shang. Two years later, he inquired of jizi the reasons for Yin's downfall.
King Wu had already overthrown Yin. Two years later, he asked Jizi why Yin had perished.
箕子 is the proper name Jizi (capitalized); 殷所以亡 asks why Yin perished.
jizi could not bring himself to speak of the Shang's wickedness, so instructed him in the principles of state survival and ruin.
Jizi could not bear to speak of Yin's evils, so he told him what preserves and ruins a state.
箕子 is the proper name Jizi and must be capitalized at sentence start.
The Duke of Zhou accepted the grain from the eastern territories and the mandate to rule Lu as the Son of Heaven.
The Duke of Zhou received the grain in the eastern lands and extolled the Son of Heaven's command.
魯 here stands for 旅 ("to display/extol"); the clause means he praised the king's command, not that he received a mandate to rule Lu as Son of Heaven.
Duke Zhao declared: 'This lies at the heart of the empire. Tribute routes from the four quarters are equally balanced in distance.'
He said: 'This is the center of the realm; the distances for tribute from the four quarters are equal.'
The silent subject continues the Duke of Zhou of s0200; the Chinese does not name Duke Zhao (the Duke of Shao) as the speaker.
Duke Zhao served as guardian, the Duke of Zhou as mentor. They campaigned eastward against the Huai barbarians, destroyed Yan, and relocated their ruler Bo Chou.
The Duke of Shao served as Guardian and the Duke of Zhou as Preceptor. They campaigned eastward against the Huai Yi, destroyed Yan, and moved its ruler to Bogu.
薄泵 (薄姑) is the place Bogu to which the ruler of Yan was moved, not the ruler's name "Bo Chou".
King Cheng having campaigned against the eastern barbarians, the Xishen came to offer congratulations. The king bestowed Rong Bo to compose the Xishen Tribute decree.
King Cheng having attacked the Eastern Yi, the Xishen came to offer congratulations. The king had Rong Bo present gifts and compose the Charge on Gifts to the Xishen.
王賜榮伯作賄息慎之命 means the king had Rong Bo (bestow gifts and) compose the charge; the English "bestowed Rong Bo" treats the person as the gift.
His passing was not immediately announced, out of deference to ritual propriety.
His death was not announced to the lords; it was concealed.
諱之 means the death was concealed as shameful, not withheld "out of deference to ritual propriety".
King Mu prepared to campaign against the Quanrong. The Earl of Ji, Mou Fu, counseled: 'This must not be done.
King Mu prepared to campaign against the Quanrong. Moufu, Duke of Zhai, remonstrated: 'This must not be done.
祭公謀父 is Moufu, Duke (公) of Zhai, not an "Earl of Ji"; 諫 means to remonstrate.
When the Xia fell into decay, they forsook Ji's teachings and grew neglectful. Our forefather Bu Xu thereby forfeited his position and concealed himself among the Rong and Di peoples.
When the Xia fell into decay, it abandoned agriculture and neglected it. Our former king Bu Xu thereby lost his office and hid himself among the Rong and Di.
棄稷不務 means the Xia abandoned the agricultural office (稷) and neglected it; it does not refer to "Ji's teachings".
King Gong was boating on the Jing River when the Marquis Kang of Mi accompanied him, and three beautiful women took refuge with the marquis.
King Gong made an outing on the Jing River, accompanied by Duke Kang of Mi, and three women eloped to the duke.
密康公 is Duke (公) Kang of Mi, not a marquis; 游 is an outing, and 奔之 means the three women eloped to him.
The king on hunts does not take entire herds, nobles in procession do not descend below crowds, kings in marriage do not wed within the same clan.
The king in hunting does not take a whole herd, a lord on the road does not dismount for a crowd, and the king's consorts do not include three from one clan.
王御不參一族 means the king does not take three consorts from a single clan; it is not about marrying within the same clan. 公行不下眾 means a lord does not dismount for a crowd.
The Marquis Kang refused to surrender them. One year later, King Gong destroyed the state of Mi.
Duke Kang did not present them. A year later, King Gong destroyed Mi.
康公 is Duke (公) Kang of Mi, not a marquis; 不獻 means he did not present them.
King Xuan neglected the field boundaries at Qianmu. Duke Wen of Guo warned this was unwise. The king paid no heed.
King Xuan did not perform the ceremonial ploughing of the royal field at Qianmu. Duke Wen of Guo remonstrated that this was wrong, but the king did not listen.
不修籍於千畝 means he did not perform the ritual ploughing of the royal field (籍田) at Qianmu, not that he neglected field boundaries.
A young concubine in the inner palace, having just reached puberty, encountered the tortoise. She became pregnant and, without a husband, bore a child. Terrified, she abandoned the infant.

A young slave girl of the inner palace had met it when she was losing her milk teeth; when she reached the age of the hairpin she became pregnant and, without a husband, bore a child. Frightened, she abandoned it.
既齔 means when she was shedding her milk teeth (a small child) and 既笄 means when she reached hairpin age; the English collapses these and mistranslates 齔 as puberty.

They fled along the road and encountered villagers—the inner palace concubine's abandoned monstrous child lying in the path. Hearing its nighttime wailing, they took pity and gathered it up. The couple then absconded, fleeing to the state of Bao.

As they fled along the road, they saw lying in the road the strange child that the palace slave girl had abandoned earlier. Hearing it cry in the night, they pitied it and took it up, and the couple fled to Bao.
鄉者 means "earlier", modifying the abandonment; it does not mean "villagers".

In the third year of King You, the women of his inner palace beheld her and adored her. She bore him a son named Bo Fu. Ultimately he deposed Queen Shen and the crown prince, installing Bao Si as queen and Bo Fu as heir.

In the third year of King You, the king saw her in his inner palace and loved her. She bore a son, Bo Fu. In the end he deposed Queen Shen and the crown prince, making Bao Si queen and Bo Fu crown prince.
王之後宮見而愛之 means the king saw her in his inner palace and loved her; it is not "the women of his inner palace" who adored her.
In King Zhuang's fourth year, the Duke Hei Jian plotted to assassinate King Zhuang and enthrone Prince Zi Ke.
In King Zhuang's fourth year, Heijian, Duke of Zhou, plotted to kill King Zhuang and enthrone Prince Ke.
周公黑肩 is Heijian, Duke of Zhou; 王子克 is Prince Ke (王子 = prince), not "Prince Zi Ke".
Prince Zi Ke fled for refuge to Yan.
王子克 is Prince Ke; "Zi" is not part of his name.
At first, King Zhuang favored his concubine Yao. She bore him a son named Sui, who was much beloved.
Earlier, King Zhuang favored his concubine Yao, who bore him a son, Tui; Tui was much favored.
穨 is read Tui (Prince Tui), not Sui.
They enthroned King Xi's younger brother Sui as king.
They enthroned King Xi's younger brother Tui as king.
穨 is read Tui, not Sui.
In the fourth year, the lords of Zheng and Guo attacked and killed King Sui, restoring King Hui to the throne.
In the fourth year, the lords of Zheng and Guo attacked and killed King Tui and restored King Hui.
王穨 is the usurper Tui, not "King Sui".
Queen Hui bore a son named Uncle Dai, who was favored by King Hui. King Xiang lived in fear of him.
Queen Hui bore Shu Dai, who was favored by King Hui; King Xiang feared him.
叔帶 is Shu Dai (Prince Dai, a younger son), not "Uncle Dai"; 叔 marks birth order.
Duke Wen of Zheng resented King Hui's restoration for not granting Duke Li his title, and resented King Xiang's gift of Wei Hua to Zheng. Thus, he imprisoned Bo Fu.
Duke Wen of Zheng resented that at King Hui's restoration Duke Li was not given a goblet, and also resented King Xiang's siding with Wei and Hua; so he imprisoned Bo Fu.
爵 here is a ritual goblet, not a title; 衛滑 is Wei and Hua, not "Wei Hua".
During the Sui rebellion, Zheng helped settle matters. Now to abandon them over petty grievances!'
In Prince Tui's revolt, it was again through Zheng that order was restored; now you would abandon them over a petty grievance!
子穨 is Prince Tui, not Sui.
At first, Queen Hui desired to enthrone Prince Zi Dai, so through her faction she invited the Di people. The Di then invaded Zhou.
Earlier, Queen Hui wanted to enthrone Prince Dai, so through her faction she opened the way for the Di, who then entered Zhou.
王子帶 is Prince Dai (Shu Dai), not "Prince Zi Dai".

King Xiang then granted Duke Wen of Jin a jade tablet, sacrificial wine, bow and arrows, made him Bo, and gave Jin the land of Henei.
河內 is the land north of the Yellow River (Henei), not "south".
In the tenth year, King Zhuang of Chu besieged Zheng. Duke Zheng surrendered, but Chu later restored him.
In the tenth year, King Zhuang of Chu besieged Zheng; the Earl of Zheng surrendered, and was afterwards restored.
鄭伯 is the Earl (ruler) of Zheng, not "Duke Zheng".
In King Jing's eighteenth year, the crown prince Sheng of the queen died prematurely.
In King Jing's eighteenth year, the queen's crown prince, a wise man, died young.
聖 here describes the crown prince as wise; it is not his name ("Sheng").
The crown prince of Duke Wu of Western Zhou died. He had five sons by concubines. None was legitimate to succeed.
Crown Prince Gong of Duke Wu of Western Zhou died; Duke Wu had five sons by concubines, none of whom was the legitimate heir.
共太子 is Crown Prince Gong (共 is his posthumous designation); the source gives no legitimate heir to install.
Qin will have no choice but to pressure Zhou not to accept, thus Han gains land from Qin while Zhou remains obedient to Qin.'
Qin will then have no grounds to make Zhou refuse; so Zhou receives land from Han while still obeying Qin.
受地於韓而聽於秦 means Zhou receives Han's land and still obeys Qin, not that Han gains land.
Dai explained: 'Giving Gaodu to Zhou will force Zhou to submit to Han. When Qin hears of this, they will rage against Zhou and cut off their envoys. Thus, with a weakened Gaodu, you preserve Zhou.
Dai said: "If you give Gaodu to Zhou, Zhou will turn and attach itself to Han; Qin will be furious with Zhou and cut off its envoys. So at the cost of a worn-out Gaodu you gain a whole Zhou."
是以獘高都得完周也: with a worthless Gaodu you obtain the whole of Zhou.
The Grand Historian remarks: Scholars all claim Zhou attacked Zhou and settled at Luoyi, but comprehensively this is not the case.
The Grand Historian says: Scholars all say that Zhou attacked King Zhou of Shang and settled at Luoyi, but on examining the facts this was not so.
紂 is King Zhou of Shang, distinct from the Zhou dynasty (周).
King Wu planned it. King Cheng had Duke Zhao divine the site and placed the nine tripods there, but Zhou made its capital Feng and Hao once more.
King Wu planned it, and King Cheng had the Duke of Shao divine the site and placed the nine tripods there, yet Zhou again made its capital at Feng and Hao.
召公 is the Duke of Shao (召 read Shao), not "Duke Zhao".

In the forty-fifth year, a Zhou envoy to Qin told Zhou Ju: 'My lord, you should praise the Qin king's filial devotion and offer Ying as land to support the dowager queen. The Qin king will be pleased, giving you influence in Qin.
In the forty-fifth year, the Zhou ruler's retainer in Qin said to Zhou Ju: "You should praise the Qin king's filial piety and offer Ying as land for the queen dowager's upkeep."
周君之秦客 is the Zhou ruler's retainer staying in Qin, not a Zhou envoy; 應 is the place Ying.
